nodes.label: Functions, Function Notation, and Multiple Representations
nodes.explanation: Assumes secondary entry background in Cartesian coordinate plotting, linear and quadratic equations and graphs, and basic algebraic substitution and factoring (from recommended preparation in Linear Functions and Systems and Quadratic Equations and Functions). Develops the concept of a function as a rule assigning each valid input in a domain exactly one output, distinguishing functions from non-function relations across tables, mapping rules, implicit equations (such as y = x² vs. x² + y² = 1 or x = y²), and graphs via the Vertical Line Test. Builds fluency with function notation y = f(x)—explicitly correcting the misconception that f(x) denotes multiplication—evaluating numeric and symbolic inputs such as f(-2), f(3a), f(x + h), and simplifying the difference quotient (f(x + h) - f(x))/h for linear and quadratic functions (without introducing limits or derivatives). Enables the learner to decide whether a relation given verbally, tabularly, algebraically, or graphically defines a function and to manipulate symbolic function evaluations cleanly. Leaves formal set-theoretic ordered-pair relations, equivalence relations, and cardinality to Sets, Relations, and Functions.

nodes.label: Domain, Range, and Natural Domain Restrictions
nodes.explanation: Builds on the function concept and evaluation to establish domain and range across algebraic, graphical, and contextual settings, supplying compact interval notation (a, b), [a, b], [a, ∞), and union ∪ directly so this tree stays self-contained without requiring Real Numbers and Inequalities as a prerequisite. Develops reading domain and range accurately from graphs with bounded, unbounded, open, and closed endpoints; computing natural (implied) domains of algebraic rules by enforcing nonzero denominators (Q(x) ≠ 0), non-negative even radicands (A(x) ≥ 0), and combined constraints (such as 1/√(x - 3) requiring strict x > 3, while ∛(x - 3) imposes no restriction); finding ranges of linear, quadratic (via vertex), and simple radical/reciprocal expressions; and applying physical domain restrictions in applied contexts. Keeps algebraic domain conditions at the linear, basic radical, and factorable-quadratic level, leaving advanced multi-factor polynomial, rational, and radical inequality machinery to Real Numbers and Inequalities. Enables the learner to determine exact domains and ranges from graphs and elementary algebraic formulas and express them cleanly in interval notation.

nodes.label: Qualitative Graph Analysis: Monotonicity, Extrema, Rate of Change, and Symmetry
nodes.explanation: Builds on domain and range to develop the standard qualitative vocabulary for analyzing functions from graphs and formulas. Defines and practices identifying x- and y-intercepts, positive and negative sign intervals, strictly increasing, strictly decreasing, and constant intervals (explicitly correcting the widespread error of reporting y-values instead of x-intervals, and clarifying open-interval reporting conventions), local (relative) vs. global (absolute) maxima and minima, boundedness (bounded above, bounded below, bounded), and average rate of change (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a) interpreted geometrically as the slope of a secant line. Develops algebraic and graphical tests for even symmetry (f(-x) = f(x), symmetry across the y-axis) and odd symmetry (f(-x) = -f(x), rotational symmetry about the origin), noting that the domain must be symmetric about 0 and that most functions are neither even nor odd. Enables the learner to produce a complete qualitative profile from a graph, compute and interpret average rates of change, and prove algebraically whether a formula is even, odd, or neither.

nodes.label: Core Elementary (Parent) Function Families
nodes.explanation: Builds on qualitative graph analysis to establish a working library of the core algebraic parent function families: constant f(x) = c, identity f(x) = x, squaring f(x) = x², cubing f(x) = x³, square root f(x) = √x, cube root f(x) = ∛x, absolute value f(x) = |x|, and the reciprocal families f(x) = 1/x and f(x) = 1/x². Systematically characterizes each family by its domain, range, key anchor points, even/odd symmetry, monotonicity intervals, end behavior, and qualitative vertical and horizontal asymptote behavior for 1/x and 1/x² (treated informally as unbounded growth or approach to a line, leaving formal limits to calculus). Compares power and root growth on (0, 1) versus (1, ∞) (highlighting why √x > x > x² on (0, 1) reverses on (1, ∞)) and trains identifying parent families from qualitative clues or rough sketches. Explicitly leaves exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric families to their dedicated trees. Enables the learner to sketch core parent functions accurately from memory and match qualitative function behavior to the appropriate parent family.

nodes.label: Piecewise-Defined and Step Functions
nodes.explanation: Builds on the core parent function families to develop reading, evaluating, graphing, and reconstructing piecewise-defined functions built from constant, linear, quadratic, root, absolute value, and reciprocal pieces. Trains matching an input to the unique branch whose domain condition it satisfies, plotting open vs. closed boundary endpoints accurately, checking that branch intervals do not assign conflicting outputs at shared boundary points, and distinguishing connected joins from jump gaps informally (leaving formal continuity and limits to calculus). Rewrites absolute value expressions such as |x - 3| or |x| + |x - 2| as piecewise linear functions, introduces step functions (tiered pricing/tax brackets and basic floor-step graphs), and extracts overall domain, range, and monotonicity intervals from piecewise graphs. Enables the learner to graph piecewise formulas, write a piecewise formula from a graph or tiered verbal specification, and verify well-definedness at boundary points.

nodes.label: Algebraic Combinations and Function Composition
nodes.explanation: Builds on domain and range to construct new functions from existing ones via pointwise arithmetic and composition. Defines (f + g)(x), (f - g)(x), (fg)(x), and (f/g)(x) with their exact domains (Dom(f) ∩ Dom(g), additionally removing all x with g(x) = 0 for quotients), and develops function composition (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)) across algebraic formulas, value tables, and graphs. Establishes non-commutativity (f ∘ g ≠ g ∘ f in general) and associativity, and centers on the critical domain bridge Dom(f ∘ g) = {x ∈ Dom(g) : g(x) ∈ Dom(f)}, exposing the classic mistake of simplifying the composite formula first (such as (√x)² = x or 1/(1/x) = x) and overlooking lost domain exclusions from the inner function g. Also trains decomposing nested expressions (such as 1/√(2x + 5) or (3x - 1)³ + 2) into simpler inner and outer components, noting that decompositions are generally not unique. Enables the learner to evaluate and simplify algebraic combinations and compositions across representations, find exact composite domains before simplification, and decompose complex formulas into layers.

nodes.label: Rigid Transformations: Translations and Reflections
nodes.explanation: Builds on the core parent function families to develop shape-preserving (rigid) graphical transformations of any function y = f(x): vertical translations f(x) + k, horizontal translations f(x - h), reflections across the x-axis -f(x), and reflections across the y-axis f(-x). Uses the input-matching bridge—asking what new coordinate x' satisfies x' - h = x, namely x' = x + h—to explain clearly why horizontal shifts move opposite to the sign inside parentheses while vertical shifts follow the sign directly. Trains tracking anchor points via coordinate rules (x, y) ↦ (x + h, y + k), (-x, y), and (x, -y) as well as tracking how domain, range, intercepts, symmetry, and vertical/horizontal asymptotes (for 1/x and 1/x²) move under rigid transformations. Works both on concrete parent families and on arbitrary unlabeled piecewise or curved graphs so the rules transfer independently of a specific formula. Enables the learner to sketch shifted and reflected graphs, write formulas from transformed graphs, and predict transformed domains, ranges, and asymptotes.

nodes.label: Stretches, Compressions, and Combined Transformations
nodes.explanation: Builds on rigid transformations to introduce non-rigid scalings—vertical scaling a·f(x) (stretch for |a| > 1, compression for 0 < |a| < 1, combined with x-axis reflection when a < 0) and horizontal scaling f(bx) (compression by 1/|b| for |b| > 1, stretch by 1/|b| for 0 < |b| < 1, combined with y-axis reflection when b < 0)—and synthesize full affine transformations y = a·f(b(x - h)) + k. Focuses on transformation order and the indispensable algebraic bridge of factoring b inside the argument, f(bx - c) = f(b(x - c/b)), so horizontal scaling and horizontal shifting are sequenced without shifting by the wrong amount; pairs this with the exact point-mapping rule (x, y) ↦ (x/b + h, ay + k) as a direct verification check. Compares cases where vertical and horizontal scalings coincide algebraically on specific parent families (such as (2x)² = 4x² or √(4x) = 2√x) against general unlabeled graphs where they produce distinct shapes. Enables the learner to graph and reconstruct any function of the form a·f(bx + c) + k in valid order and map key points, domains, ranges, and asymptotes reliably.

nodes.label: Absolute-Value Transformations: |f(x)| and f(|x|)
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes piecewise functions with combined graph transformations to develop the two non-linear absolute-value graph operations y = |f(x)| and y = f(|x|). Uses piecewise rewriting as the exact algebraic bridge: |f(x)| equals f(x) where f(x) ≥ 0 and -f(x) where f(x) < 0 (retaining points on or above the x-axis while reflecting negative portions upward across the x-axis, often creating sharp corners at x-intercepts), whereas f(|x|) equals f(x) for x ≥ 0 and f(-x) for x < 0 (discarding the left half of the graph and mirroring the x ≥ 0 branch across the y-axis to produce an even function). Contrasts |f(x)|, f(|x|), and |f(|x|)| on parent families, transformed functions (such as |1/(x - 1) - 2| or (|x| - 1)² - 4), and abstract graphs, emphasizing how order with shifts and reflections changes the resulting curve (for example, |f(x) - 2| vs. |f(x)| - 2). Enables the learner to sketch and interpret graphs involving outer and inner absolute values and determine their resulting domains, ranges, and symmetries.

nodes.label: Injectivity (One-to-One Functions) and Monotonicity
nodes.explanation: Builds on qualitative graph analysis and monotonicity to develop injectivity (the one-to-one property) as the exact condition governing invertibility of functions. Defines a function f to be one-to-one when f(x₁) = f(x₂) implies x₁ = x₂ (equivalently, distinct inputs always map to distinct outputs), connects this directly to the Horizontal Line Test on graphs, and trains the two-sided testing workflow: proving injectivity algebraically by solving f(x₁) = f(x₂) for x₁ = x₂, versus disproving injectivity with a single explicit counterexample pair x₁ ≠ x₂ giving f(x₁) = f(x₂). Proves that every strictly increasing or strictly decreasing function on an interval is automatically one-to-one, while exhibiting a piecewise or disconnected-domain counterexample (such as 1/x on ℝ \ {0}) showing that a one-to-one function need not be globally monotonic. Explicitly leaves surjectivity, bijections between abstract sets, and cardinality to Sets, Relations, and Functions. Enables the learner to prove or refute injectivity algebraically and graphically and use strict monotonicity as a rapid injectivity test.

nodes.label: Inverse Functions: Existence, Computation, and Reflection Geometry
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes function composition with injectivity to establish the inverse function f⁻¹ of a one-to-one function f. Defines f⁻¹ rigorously via the two cancellation identities f⁻¹(f(x)) = x for all x ∈ Dom(f) and f(f⁻¹(y)) = y for all y ∈ Dom(f⁻¹), explicitly dismantling the pervasive notational misconception that f⁻¹(x) means the reciprocal 1/f(x). Establishes the exact domain-range swap (Dom(f⁻¹) = Range(f) and Range(f⁻¹) = Dom(f)) and the reflection symmetry of the graphs of f and f⁻¹ across the line y = x via coordinate swapping (a, b) ↔ (b, a). Trains computing algebraic inverses of linear, odd-power/odd-root, shifted-radical, and linear fractional rational functions (ax + b)/(cx + d) (carrying the domain restriction carefully), finding inverse values from tables and graphs without a formula, and verifying candidate inverse pairs by checking both compositions. Enables the learner to determine when an inverse exists, compute and sketch f⁻¹, verify inverses via composition, and deduce domains and ranges of inverses directly from f.

nodes.label: Domain Restrictions, Branch Inverses, and Inverses of Composites
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes combined transformations with inverse functions to handle non-injective functions via domain restriction and analyze how inverses interact with composition and transformations. Develops restricting non-one-to-one functions—especially transformed quadratics a(x - h)² + k and absolute-value branches—to maximal intervals of strict monotonicity (such as x ≥ h vs. x ≤ h) so an inverse branch exists, using the sign of x - h on the restricted domain as the key bridge to select the correct radical branch (+√ vs. -√) and verify that Range(f⁻¹) matches the restricted Dom(f). Establishes the reversal ('socks-and-shoes') law (f ∘ g)⁻¹ = g⁻¹ ∘ f⁻¹ for invertible functions and applies it to invert transformed expressions a·f(b(x - h)) + k step by step, connecting this geometrically to how reflection across y = x converts horizontal transformations of f into vertical transformations of f⁻¹ and vice versa. Enables the learner to construct branch inverses with matching sign choices and domain/range bounds, and to invert composite and transformed functions structurally.

nodes.label: General Line/Point Symmetry and Even-Odd Decomposition
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment synthesizing algebraic function combinations with rigid transformations (and using even/odd symmetry from earlier ancestors) to generalize symmetry beyond the coordinate axes. Develops exact functional equations for reflection symmetry across an arbitrary vertical line x = a (f(a + t) = f(a - t), equivalently f(2a - x) = f(x)) and 180-degree rotational symmetry about an arbitrary point (a, b) (f(a + t) + f(a - t) = 2b, equivalently f(2a - x) + f(x) = 2b), verifying them on shifted quadratics, cubics, and hyperbolas such as 1/(x - 2) + 3. Proves the unique even-odd decomposition theorem: every function f defined on a domain symmetric about 0 splits uniquely as f(x) = f_even(x) + f_odd(x), where f_even(x) = (f(x) + f(-x))/2 and f_odd(x) = (f(x) - f(-x))/2, proving both existence and uniqueness cleanly by evaluating at -x. Enables the learner to test general axes and centers of symmetry algebraically and decompose arbitrary functions into their unique even and odd parts.

nodes.label: Fixed Points, Function Iteration, and Self-Inverse Functions
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment building on inverse functions and composition to explore repeated composition fⁿ = f ∘ f ∘ ... ∘ f, fixed points f(x) = x, and involutions (self-inverse functions satisfying f(f(x)) = x on their domain). Connects fixed points geometrically to intersections of y = f(x) with the diagonal y = x, demonstrating why any intersection of f and f⁻¹ on y = x is a fixed point while showing via counterexamples (such as f(x) = -x³ or f(x) = 1 - x) that f and f⁻¹ can also intersect in symmetric off-diagonal pairs (a, b) and (b, a) when f(f(a)) = a. Characterizes classic elementary involutions—such as c - x, k/x, and linear fractional maps (ax + b)/(cx - a) with a² + bc ≠ 0—by their symmetry across y = x, and introduces basic graphical iteration (cobwebbing between y = f(x) and y = x) for linear and simple nonlinear rules without formal dynamical-systems stability theory. Enables the learner to find fixed points, test whether a function is an involution, and trace short iterates both algebraically and graphically.
